t: Section 2(e)(1)(B) of Public Law 109–129 shall be applied by substituting the date specified in section 106(3) of this Act for “September 30, 2010”.

fable.w: This section only substitutes a date in a cross-referenced provision of Public Law 109-129, which is a purely technical extension. The tempting reading is that the referenced law might involve some outside-party process, but nothing in this text itself calls for consultation, comment, hearings, advisory bodies, rulemaking, or a right to sue involving anyone outside the federal government.

opus.w: This section is a date substitution, the kind found in a continuing resolution: it extends a deadline in Public Law 109–129 by replacing "September 30, 2010" with a date set elsewhere in the Act. No one outside the federal government is consulted or involved in any federal decision. A Yes reading would depend only on whatever the cross-referenced law contains, and nothing in this text itself creates a way for outside parties to take part.

qwen_chat.w: This section is a technical amendment that substitutes one date for another in a referenced statute. It does not establish any mechanism for consultation, comment, or coordination with parties outside the federal government. There is no mention of public hearings, advisory committees, or rights to sue, nor does it involve any interaction with states, tribes, or the public.
qwen_chat.s: Section 2(e)(1)(B) of Public Law 109–129 shall be applied by substituting the date specified in section 106(3) of this Act for “September 30, 2010”.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that changing a date in a statute could affect a comment period or deadline for public participation. However, the text itself is merely a technical amendment to a date reference and contains no language establishing, requiring, or describing any process for public or outside-party participation. It does not mention hearings, comments, advisory boards, or consultations with non-federal entities.
